game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

You can jail people for their internet posts and for what they said in private conversations. 
1984 out of 10.
[spoiler]

The irony is, this "future" is already here. You can actually go in jail for this stuff in russia and china.
So i guess you could say this is pretty hot topic.

After all, there is no god or devil. Only man.[/spoiler]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]General[/h1]

This is [b]not really a game.[/b] Most of the time you would only be pointing out "data chunks" to relevant character, and the said data chunks has been conveniently pointed out to you by the highlight, so you can't miss it. The only time you get a little pressure is on the final episode, when there are "data upload" limit imposed on you.

[h1]There is minimal gameplay[/h1]
There is minimal gameplay, as it is mostly just drag and drop something. The clues are too easily pointed out to you. Sometimes there are some conflicting data, but it is easy to resolve this kind of things. It is also bad that you don't know how the data chunks you are given is processed. A wrong data chunk could suddenly net a very violent response although previous data chunks you have given it is not the way. 


[h1]Story-Rich Gameplay[/h1]
However, the story in the game is excellent. It is not overly long and complicated, but it is quite complicated enough to keep you guessing on who is who and what is the truth beneath all of these things. All of the characters are alive, and the way they are chatting with each other, with you snooping in, at times make you guilty for snooping on someone's conversation. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a fun, engaging, clever, brilliant, unique game that I would say is a mix of L.A. Noire, Her Story, Papers Please, and a touch of Telltale Games thrown in.

You go about solving a main crime which, along the way, you will discover a group of characters--all suspects. You do this by examining, accessing, reading through, and hacking into many different kinds of online resources (this would be the 'Her Story' aspect of it: A game where you get bits of the story unlocked, piece by piece and out of order, over time). As you go on, you will learn more and more about the suspects and characters and you need to try to figure out what information is relevant and what is not. What points of info is truth and what is false. What bits of knowledge and writings and conjectures are sarcasm or jokes and what is being said with true belief.... (the LA Noire side of it). Can you read between the lines and use logic and intuition to decide what will help you with the case and what may NOT be so smart to share with the database? 
You see, what you share with the database is totally up to you. This is the TellTale Game and Papers, Please side of it... in Papers, Please, you had the option, sometimes, to break the rules or turn your head to things based on what you believed to be morally right or true..or even just due to personal hunches or gut feelings.  What you choose to forever put into the database will affect the story, characters, and outcomes in a big way...there are multiple ways things could play out depending on if characters are free, in jail, or even killed. Sometimes you even have choices to make in the spur of the moment. Events that will happen in a few minutes (in game time) that you can either stop or allow to happen to see how things play out.


...but once you choose to document something into the database, the die is cast and you must live with your choices and  then all you can do is sit back and watch things play out and hopefully not live to regret how it all turned out.

Would strongly recommend.

review_text_raw:
I had a pretty good idea of what to expect when I started playing Orwell, but I was surprised time and time again about the absolutely amazing writing and the whole premise of the game. While not being overly complex in its mechanics, Orwell provides an emotional experience like few other games I have ever played and is able to capture the dystopian vibe of 1984 to an extremely disturbing level.

I started my first playthrough in the evening and it gripped me so much that I couldn't stop playing until I had finished the game some time around 3 a.m.

While the game doesn't offer a lot of choices, most of these actually do matter and then fold out in a logical way. Contrary to Telltale games, choices have an actual emotional impact on the player, which is something I haven't seen often in videogaming.

Everyone even remotely interested in storytelling and the workings of society should have played this to completion at least once. Especially people who think they have nothing to hide and don't see an issue with the paradigm of security above all. This game does actually successfully deliver a very disturbing perspective.

review_text_raw:
I've had bad experiences with plot-heavy games. Even Telltale's much celebrated titles did very little for me and have contributed to this theory I've had for a long time to video games, in general, seemed incapable of telling a good story. I've always believed that games were much stronger when focusing on mechanics, and those that sacrificed mechanics in favor of plot would always just create an inferior work compared to books or movies.

Orwell is an exception.

What at first might strike you as a fairly preachy "topic of the day" game managed to surpass all my expectations. From the beginning till the end, Orwell and it's characters captivated me.

Orwell is an elegant game. One that understands perfectly how to integrate the agency of it's players to fit into the narrative it's trying to weave, and does so well. Despite the fact that you simply play as a man behind a computer screen, your actions feel like they have consequences, even if sometimes those consequences are ones you don't intend. The longer I played the game, the more I thought about the consequences of every piece of information I submitted, pouring over every bit of data and agonizing over the tiniest nuances of dialogue

While Orwell's themes should be fairly evident from it's title and presentation, I found the plot to be intelligent and far from one-dimensional. Playing the game, often I thought to myself: "Did I make the right call?", "Should I really have told them about that?" I spent a good thirty minutes trying to decide on what I would do during the ending, and even as I write this review I question if I really did the right thing.

To me, that is the hallmark of a good story. One that engages you, makes you feel invested...and above all else; makes you care. It's been a while since I felt so compelled to write a recommendation. But Orwell is one of these games that comes once in a blue moon, and tend to get sadly overlooked. If you couldn't guess already, I highly recommend Orwell. It's one of the best experiences I've had with a story rich game to date, Osmotic Studios has done a fantastic job.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

P.S. Once you exit Orwell, you are greeted by advertisement of a sequel - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength. Fear not though, Keeping an Eye On You provides a complete storyline, no “to be continued” ending attached.

review_text_raw: Orwell is OKAY. Not great, but I enjoyed the experience for what it was; a visual novel. To be frank, the story basically plays itself out. You're just a passenger in this ride. The actual simulation of being an "investigator" is not fulfilled here whatsoever. Everything you can take note of is already highlighted for you. This is the gaming equivalent of sticking wooden blocks in their appropriate holes. It's a shame a political story as convoluted and detailed as Orwell's is matched with mindless "gameplay". I enjoyed the unique approach to storytelling and seeing the plot unravel with many twists and turns was engrossing. However, having your advisor constantly chime in after every single datachunk is submitted is annoying and unnecessary. There's no in-depth deduction system like the Sherlock Holmes games. Everything is filled in and connected for you. I find the topics of surveillance, civil unrest, immigration, etc. very fascinating, but to have the game straight up tell you what the right and wrong choices are takes away from the experience imo. I don't need the game to wag its finger at me for deciding that the terrorists belong in prison. The lack of nuance in how your very few choices are reflected in the end feels patronizing. In reality, with or without Orwell, there would be massive consequences. It's a very complex discussion, but the game ends before any discussion can really be had rushing through the final episode with a sloppy "I think we should do this, BUT IT'S UP TO YOU [insert player name here]!" choice at the end that just feels unearned. The concept and strong premise drew me in and the mystery kept me to the end. If you value deep forensics gameplay, look elsewhere. If you want a fairly compelling political thriller, this is not bad for the price. (6/10)

review_text_raw:
[quote][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/7871885/]Follow our curator page:[b] OCG-Curations[/b] if you like and want to see more reviews like this one.[/url][/quote]

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
Orwell takes place in a distopian near future in the fictional city of Bonton in The Nation. Orwell is the codename of a vastly advanced surveilance system. They outsource investigations to outsiders of the nation - you! It is your task to spy on suspects and inform the government of what is going on. Basically, you roleplay as "Mr. FBI Man".

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Interesting Story[/b] - The game is divided into five chapters, each representing a day in game. I won't be spoiling anything here so there isn't much to say, but I will state my overall impression. The story is good! If you take everything at face value you'll be in for a surprise when you realise this game is not as shallow as it may seem. Each chapter unveils another layer of mystery. There are also three endings (more on that later).

[*][b]Some Replayability[/b] - Every chapter has a few endings (usually two or three). After you finish the game, you may choose to replay starting from any chapter (subsequent ones are erased). Most unique paths you can take are linked to an achievement, so 100%-ing the game is pretty much just exploring every possibility. Don't get too exited though, as that took me about 8 hours and two playthroughs (but in the second one I did consult a guide to save time).

[*][b]Clean UI[/b] - I really like the clean, very intuitive interface. Which is good, considering as this UI is basically the whole game itself. The only downside is that it does not have a dark mode for playing at night, but it's not a dealbreaker.
[/list]

[h1]The Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Hand Holding[/b] - You give information to Orwell by drag and dropping data chunks from your spy browser to the Orwell app. They are automatically outlined for you, which seems stupid, but it's a necesarry evil if you think about the programmers. However, one thing I don't like are the special chunks - the conflicts are highlighted in yellow, even if you didn't find both. This makes you extra careful before uploading as one makes the other invalid. This is how the story branches, but if you think about it it's a little stupid. How does the browser know about the conflict if you didn't access the other data chunk yet? This should be up to you - the "detective" to figure out. I wish they were all blue all the time, or turn yellow only after discovering both.

[*][b]Choices Almost Don't Matter[/b] - Remember when I said chapters? Well... they're pretty much isolated instances. Outcomes are mentioned from one to another, but only through slight dialogue changes. But the story progresses the same no matter what you do, until you reach chapter five and finally get to choose an ending.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Orwell is a good game because it explores an interesting concept and offers a good story to boot. While it's not as mindbending as I first expected, I still recommended it as a very interactive visual novel. If the topic interests you and don't mind the short playtime, this is a good game to pick up.

This is basically a super-clever way of telling a story but making you feel like you are in control. In reality there are a couple of ways it can play out, but you are still following a storyline.

In some ways, it is like Bandersnatch for those of you familiar with it.

We had a BLAST playing this and are looking forward to trying out the future installments. Great job doing this and hopefully it will teach a new generation some of the terrors that come along with George Orwell's writings.

If you have never read 1984 and Animal Farm, you owe it to yourself to watch the movies, read the books or find some way to consume them that you enjoy. Like Ayn Rand's Anthem, Atlas Shrugged and Fountainhead, they are important stories to have at least given some thought.

review_text_raw: Before buying this game, I saw that most of the top rated reviews just spoke about comparison's to Orwellian works, modern social networks, and Papers Please. And I thought important to address a couple of things after playing through what is available. Orwell is an episodic game; meaning, this is not the final result. This is more of a "Whodunit" than a Thriller mystery, so judging it for linearity might be unfair since they attempt to make you the detective by providing you with a given set of aesthetics. Now talking about aesthetics, this game/experience has its obvious references to Orwell and "1984" -- mainly -- but it is very clear they are only used for inspiration. This is no de facto Orwell Fan Fiction, just an experienced based on some questions the devs had about resembling aspects of society. From the two episodes they have released, I can tell that this is comparable to Papers Please in that you have to provide an analysis to come up with game altering decisions. However, since this is a "Whodunit" type mystery, and are limited to less than half of the intended story arc, we cannot truly make that comparison. What I can say without spoiling, is that there are choices that can either save or spare hundreds of lives, and the deciding factor is actually a juxtaposition of logic I have yet to fully grasp and understand. I think this is a great game; yet, it remains an aesthetic experience we are not yet able to finalise. I look forward for Episode 3's release in three day's time.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The dystopian future is upon us. In it, we are tasked with examining all the various data about the target person - their communication, medical reports, posts on social sites, etc.; as all of the information can help us in protecting The Nation and its citizens.
When terror strikes in the heart of the capital, the [i]Orwell[/i] and we with it are put on the front line. With only one suspect at the beginning, we need to search throughout their data for any possible hints that could lead us to the truth about the attacks and the culprits behind them. But more suspects mean more information to get lost in and recognizing what info is relevant will put our deduction skills to a challenge. Also, anything inserted into [i]Orwell[/i] can't be taken back, and even the smallest information can cause a disaster.

Be prepared to read a lot in this game - there is tons of information and every new connection will add more to the ever-growing pile. You don't have to read everything if you don't feel like it, but if you do, you will know more. Simple as that. It can be quite enjoyable to peek into what people share about them on the internet… not very ethical from me, but when else would I have the opportunity? :P
The interface is simple - we are operating in a program that allows us to browse the internet, listen to phone conversations or control a suspect's PC/phone. From all of the information we pick up interesting data and attach it to the respective person. Some data will open new information sources, some are irrelevant or completely wrong, and some are in conflict with each other - from those we need to select the one we deem to be right. Those are the important ones that will influence how the story progress.

What bothered me was the fact that the phone calls can't be skipped or hastened in any way. So other runs for the remaining achievements were a little bit painful. Also, the replayability is somehow dubious - you can take a different approach and frame someone else, but otherwise it's still the same - you need to go through the same talks, lines, everything.

Although I am not much into political stuff and this is full of political talks, I have rather enjoyed it. Through Orwell you can firsthand experience how easily can information be twisted around… not that we don't know already in this age, right?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The true strength of Orwell lies not in replayability, or even in a strong gameplay mechanic, but in a consuming immersion that relays a story illustrating how powerful a government powered by surveillance could truly be.  You "live" what it would really mean to the lives of people you begin to learn more and about as you coldly monitor them in what feels like real time. 

Unlike other games employing immersive story driven simulations on rails, like "This is the Police" or Uplink, I never once sought to find a "right" solution online.  I accepted that my data was only as good as the research I could see in front of me, and I made some calls based on the psychology of the subjects I digitally (legally) stalked, for the good of The Nation.  By the middle of the game, I couldn't really stop.  It was like binging Netflix, and although pulling back I can clearly see that the game is often holding your hand and guiding you towards the next arc, in the moment the progression feels so natural that I was just excited to unravel the next thread. I performed my role in the Orwell program compliantly. 

The music and the Minority Report style slick UI (that felt so good to work in), combined with the friendly banter of your friendly government advisor led me to the worst part about this game - I started it at 11pm.  I had work at 8am the next day, which only allowed a couple hours of sleep after finally beating the game over 6 straight hours.  

There are unique endings, and the game will bend based on your choices and how far you dig.  When investigating, you don't have to read deeply into every article - Orwell finds the pertinent data for you so you're not forced to muddle through what turns into a mountain of documentation.  Sometimes though, you really need to step back and figure out your suspects murder mystery style, except you do it by going through their files, emails, phone call transcripts, timelines, and chat logs - tying that in with publically available resources. 

And maybe that's the biggest lesson of the game, and of 1984 when you apply a technical layer - in a society where we are constantly generating documents and digital paper trails, you could really learn all you need to know to paint us as however you'd like with the right tools.  It's one thing to read it, but the game lets you feel it. All at once it was exciting, and chilling.

In the end, without offering spoilers, the game never forces you to choose if this is right or wrong.

The total time to beat the game, for me, was 5 hours, but hardly any of that was spent idle. For $10 (I got this on sale at $6), if you have even half the experience I did, the game proves its value quickly.  While you can only replay the game the same way you would reread a book (altered maybe slightly), it did give me a short story worth thinking about for much longer than the gameplay itself lasted.


Pros:

- Immersive gameplay and story
- Great soundtrack
- UI feels fantastic
- Great value
- Story ending felt wrapped up, not abrupt

Cons:

- Limited replayability
- 5 hours of content (I take the time to read a lot of the docs)
- Not super challenging to an average player

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
You know all those safety measures we usually take (or fail to take online) for fear our personal info may be compromised and exploited by the powers that be? Well, Orwell puts you in the shoes of one of those people who collect such data. An outsourced data processor hired by the government.
Most of the time you will be selecting data chunks and uploading them to the mainframe of a huge, centralised surveillance hub. This explains both the concept and the mechanics of the game. The game is not linear and the story branches depending on your choices.

The story is fairly engaging, but the questions and dilemmas that the game deals with are even more compelling. If you are interested in the matters of online privacy, online identity, laws on privacy, data collecting engines or even just dystopia in general, this is a game for you.

That said, the game has its shortcomings in that the story, when you find out all the bits, does not really always add up in the most logical of ways, particularly if you choose some of the more exotic routes of the story.

Still, the experience itself is fairly novel, so this one gets an unreserved recommendation.

There’s something oddly calming about these kinds of games. No button-mashing, no reflex tests, no “oops I fell off the roof again” moments. Just me, a cup of coffee, a comfy chair, and the soft hum of moral ambiguity.

Orwell lets you dig, decide, and doubt. It’s like being a digital detective with a slight caffeine addiction and an increasing concern for how twisted “logic” can get when filtered through surveillance systems and personal bias.
You’ll click around, feel clever, feel conflicted – and occasionally yell at the screen because "wait, that’s not what I meant!"

But do I regret anything?
Absolutely not. That’s the beauty of it: different choices, different outcomes, different little identity crises.

Highly recommend if you enjoy quiet intensity, ethical dilemmas, and feeling both powerful and powerless at the same time.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Review originally posted [url=https://www.backlog-assassins.net/posts/z7q2vd7/]here[/url].

9/10

This was a hell of a game. It’s one of an emerging genre of… ‘interface’ games, I guess. Like Her Story, you are literally your character in the game - what you see on screen is what your character sees, and you interact in the same way. Because of this, the game is incredibly immersive and therefore, at points, really tense!

Let me stop myself before I get too deep in here. In Orwell, you play as, ostensibly, yourself, hired as an ‘investigator’ in this new program called Orwell situated in a different country. In that country, a bomb has just exploded in a plaza, killing two and wounding a dozen or so people. Moments before the bomb went off, a woman was spotted crossing the plaza and getting on a bus. That woman had been arrested months before for assaulting a police officer in that very same plaza during a protest. Could she be connected to the bomb? Your task is to slowly collect information on her, and the people around her. What information you upload to the system cannot be taken back, and you get to choose what the narrative of what happened becomes. You can take an innocuous joke between friends and upload it, taking it out of a friendly context and giving it a sinister cast. You can shift a bias on a person by only uploading the worst of what they said, but not uploading good things about them. In this story, YOU are the faceless watcher, the cog in the wheel, that would be impeding the heroes of a more traditional story.

Holy shit, does it work.

I blasted through the game’s five chapters in one sitting, about four and a half hours on Saturday night. Nobody in this game is 100% good or bad, and there’s a lot of nuance around protesting for the ‘right’ reason in the ‘right’ way that is especially topical for me, right now, as a young woman living in an America I never really thought I’d be living in. This game doesn’t deliver any hard and fast morals at the end, it doesn’t take a definitive stance, and offers three different endings for the player to eventually pick. The game offers up a scenario and leaves it up to you to decide what you think is right… or at least, what you think is the least wrong.

The game isn’t perfect - it wears a little thin when you’re going back and achievement gathering. Like a Telltale game, once you see the constraints of the ‘world’ of the game, the illusion dissipates pretty quickly. There are a lot of real-time sections (text conversations, phone calls) that, while immersive the first time around, made me really wish I had a fast forward button for the fourth or fifth time I sat through the conversation. These are absolutely small gripes, however, and I would strongly urge anyone to pick up this game - especially while it’s still on sale.

The message is pretty much predictable, and while you might have certain doubts/hopes in the beginning that there will be arguments for both sides - spoilers - well, there are none.

UI is a little clunky, the characters are mostly annoying stereotypical millenials, and, frankly, fuck me for spending 5 hours on it, I do have - simply more fun - things to do in my life. But, funnily enough, I felt compelled to finish it, so then again, maybe it's not so bad?..

That all said, I have no idea why there's a season 2, except for the dev wanting more monies, especially having seen the ending(s) and all.

Will I be playing season 2? - oh fuck no.

review_text_raw:
A somewhat naive anti-surveillance game when it comes to messaging, but considering I'm stating this with hindsight and the many things that both happened and have been revealed since 2016 and the unimpeded expansion of mass surveillance, the naivete is only seen now. Otherwise, an interesting investigation game, though there were several moments that had me annoyed as I would have conflicting datachunks that actually didn't change anything, and simultaneously inoffensive-looking information that would flip the whole plot. 
I think, as a concept, Orwell is great, but the slightly railroad-y execution somewhat holds it back from being genuinely great. Leaving more autonomy for the player to figure things out themselves and go after red herrings or get stuck in logical loops and unimportant information would improve the gameplay. In fact, Orwell does exactly this in the last act by limiting the amount of information that can be processed.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell, in a not-so-subtle nod to George Orwell's criticism of totalitarianism (*CoughCommunismCough*) 1984. I've actually read 1984. It's not bad. It's not great, and quite frankly I think it's more of an observation than a story which in my eyes weakens it. It's also an incredibly quick read so I do recommend you check it out. On a scale of 1-10? Probably a 7. Amusing, but not the best. Slightly better than average.

Anyway, the gameplay of Orwell is unconventional and reminds me greatly of Papers, Please. Which is another game I should write a review on and I do recommend it. In it you scan documents for information and upload this information into a mega-database which contains details on everyone under investigation (at this time). Presumably, Orwell would be expanded to cover all citizens. In the name of peace, surely! Everyone can trust the government to know every detail about them to make sure that they're entirely safe! 

Light Spoiler Warning: Orwell is a narrative, a visual novel of sorts. I'm going to do my best to avoid spoilers.

Throughout the course of Orwell you follow the individuals of an organization called 'Thought' named after some German poem. Thought is an alleged terrorist organization. Your job is to follow the members of this organization to prevent terrorist activity. The first person you investigate is a woman with blue hair and problem glasses because of course she is. Which now presents us with our question. What scale of authoritarianism would be acceptable in the name of protecting people? As the game progresses, it gets to the point where almost the slightest connection to someone (perhaps eating lunch or seeing a movie together) is grounds for investigation. Authoritarianism seems to have a very tough job reigning itself in from being conventionally oppressive. 

You know, I could not help but giggle with glee as I listened to phone calls of people and other people got blamed for things that I did. It was glorious! And it kept happening! I felt no guilt at all for doing my job. Perhaps that's the point of the game. Thinking.jpg

The art style is... quirky. Not bad. Just quirky. The music is pretty okay too. My (small) gripe (I guess) is how long I had to wait for responses when it came to monitoring calls and SMS. I get that it's supposed to be realistic, that's the point. Not really a point against the game, I just felt that it was sometimes a little long. 

Overall, excellent game. Quite a nice length for the price ($10 at the time of posting). Of course, cheaper is always better. I think my first playthrough had a run of about 4 hours and there are multiple endings (all of which, I did not explore). It's a thumbs up from me.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell stars you, the player, as an investigator in the Nation's (a stand-in for an unholy almagamation of the United States and the United Kingdom) new, government-ordained spying programme. Your job is to investigate suspected terrorists and cherrypick data you've acquired via researching the Internet and spying directly on their conversations, phones, and computers. You upload these data modules to the Orwell database and help construct a profile of these suspects that your advisor (who can't see your research sources in an effort to maintain some sort of ethical loophole) then uses to report back to the authorities, thus causing your actions to have potentially devastating consequences.

I've seen a few people complain about the gameplay--you are, essentially, dragging these data modules from one part of your screen to another (and, frustratingly, it can take a few clicks to get hold of them), which sounds unexciting on paper. But the story is compelling, and it's through this (slightly repetitive and boring) gameplay that you unlock the story, which can branch depending on which data you upload to Orwell. Some of it you have to, some of it you don't--and some of it you can use to alter the perception of certain suspects by picking which element of contradicting data you want to show to the advisor. 

The game does a very good job of highlighting how people become complacent with this level of privacy invasion--I've seen complaints of the game handholding you throughout, but, in my opinion, this helps you to slip into the mindset of uploading whatever data you come across, mindlessly painting suspects as victims because it's what your advisor wants of you. It wasn't until the end of my first playthrough that I realised how much damage I'd caused by providing evidence to suggest that innocent people were guilty of crimes they hadn't committed, and how many of the characters I'd either had arrested or killed via my actions of "innocuously" collecting their data. Which I guess is what the game wants you to do, particularly on a first playthrough.

That's not to say I don't have complaints. The game wants you to play multiple playthroughs, even if only to collect all of the achievements (most of which can be acquired in two playthroughs; two require a third, or replaying chapters on one of your profiles). Different actions have different outcomes and dialogue, and that produces slightly new scenes to watch (or, really, read). The problem is that the texts and calls you have to monitor can be so tediously long, particularly with little deviation--the last chapter has one that's just about shy of 10 minutes, and you can't do anything but sit and let it play. There's no option to skip the scene. 

I've also seen a few people complain that the game thinks people can never lie or exaggerate, which I assume refers to options where you can report suspects for having outspoken anti-government tendencies... but again, I think this is overlooking what the game wants you to consider. 

I highly recommend Orwell, although I bought it in the Humble Bundle and so bought it for much cheaper than its standard price--and I've already collected all the achievements in just over 6 hours of play, which isn't quite a £1 = 1 hour of playtime at its normal price. It's obviously not a game that's appealing to everyone, but I do think for those that like immersive visual novels with political themes (and that's essentially what it is), you'll enjoy Orwell.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This a pretty clever little narrative game. 

You essentially play the role of an investigator using a survelliance software system called Orwell, and investigate people that are citizens of a country referred to as "The Nation", that seems to be modeled off of present day Western nations like the US, UK, Canada etc. You don't have total access to everything, as your adviser often needs to 'get clearance' to add someone to the target list, but you still wield a chilling amount of investigative power eventually. 

This is not set in an extreme totalitarian world like the state of Oceania in [i]1984[/i], but a mostly present day world. It's a bit ambiguous though, as a couple real countries are referred to eventually, and 'The Nation' has some ominous things about it that suggest a veiled totalitarianism, especially with references to 'The Party'.  

There isn't alot of 'gameplay' to it, as you basically just use the mouse to collect bits of information on people from your various electronic sources. It's UI is basically the same ideas as using a computer and web browser.  

While all selectable information is highlighted for you, you do have to make decisions about what information to upload to a person's Orwell profile, and that can have major consequences for events in the story.  Some info is obviously useful, some is just mundane, some bits of info conflict with others. With the conflicting info though, i wish there were sometimes more avaliable info to make a better judgement, but I guess that's the point. 

There are at least a few different endings, but you may have to do a full playthrough again to get them, i'm not sure. 

Without giving away any spoilers to the story, there is a persistent (and i'm sure intentional) irony about the people you are tasked to investigate.  The in-game stated purpose of Orwell and your position is to protect the nation from terrorist threats.  The story starts off when a small bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza.  From that point, the network of people you investigate are all tied to the ideology of wanting privacy. Basically, you are doing the exact things that are fueling this ideology. 

This is excellent social and political commentary in the form of a simple game, and I would definitetly recommend it!

Personally I wouldn't hesitate to give this game 10/10. Loved the concept, loved the gameplay, and the story is one of the best I've played, it's so cleverly written. 

Who the game is for: 
Anyone who likes an excellent story well told with plenty of twists and red herrings
Anyone who likes games that give a message but don't shove it down your throat
Anyone who likes games with consequences to your actions
Anyone who just likes the thought of snooping characters emails, blogs, computers etc
Anyone who digs dystopian near future fiction and conspiracies, or who likes to solve a good mystery.

Anyone who only enjoys action/platforming/FPS/RTS (I like all these, but this game is nothing like them, I guess that's obvious though!)
Anyone with no patience, who doesn't like reading in games, or spending the time to really dig into things.

The price (even not on sale) is more than fair for the depth and work that has gone into making this mini masterpiece (if you rush through, you could spend maybe 4 hours, if you take your time and try and dig into all the information, closer to 8-9 hours). It really pushes the boundaries of story telling within games, and the thrill of coming up with ideas, possibilities, then to change them totally (or not) based off of a piece of information you didnt think was relevant earlier is a real highlight). 

As someone else has said in their review, don't do too much digging into the story before playing, approach the game with an open mind and allow the story and gameplay to take root, play the game your own way.  

Basically, if anything at all about the trailers or game information intrigues you, I wouldnt hesitate to recommend it. You won't regret it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Now, when I went into Orwell, I was fairly certain of what I would be getting out of my experience. An interesting little narrative set in an Orwellian-universe where you help figure out who perpetrated a terrorist attack. In a way, that's exactly what I got. But, looking back on my time with the game, I'm struck by how utterly wrong I was. Orwell exceeds all expectations and leaves me itching to either give the game another go, or threaten the developers at knife point to let me play Season 2, which the game helpfully reminded me to add to my wishlist before exiting the program.

I'm sure there's some connection that can be made to the game monitoring me in that last sentence, but I'll let it slide because Orwell deserves all the levity I can grant it.

Addressing the actual game instead of gushing all over my laptop and nearby furniture, it plays out as a sort of Point-and-Click adventure game where websites, conversations, and remote connections act as different areas, and datablocks act as items. The real twist is that, once you collect a new piece of information, there is no undo button. Your supervisor can only see what you let him see, and you can't take any information back if you realize you made a bad call or acted too hastily. And the game makes you live with it. After making a particularly blatant error, I fell back into bad habbits and attempted to quit the game and allow myself another go from whatever autosave the game keeps. 

Unfortunately for my inner gaming sins, Orwell knows exactly where you left off, as the exit screen likes to remind you. If you mess up, you've messed up permanently on that file. Wanna redo? Looks like you're starting over.

This knowledge that everything you do will have intentional and unintentional consequences makes this the most tense and nerve wracking narrative experience i've played in quite some time. This is especially apparent in the final act, which I won't be spoiling because everyone needs to experience the game's final twists and turns for themselves.

As much as I love the game, it isn't entirely without flaws. Some of the indicators for new information disappear too quickly, forcing me to search through articles trying to locate missing data. There are times where the information you need to use to progress the investigation is incredibly obscure, sending you on another hidden picture adventure. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell depicts a utopian setting where individual privacy is constantly violated thanks to public cyber-surveillance in form of an eponymous system, and justified through an ambiguous "Safety Bill" that sanctions "investigative methods" in order to "protect the freedom of The Nation's citizens."
Just how the knowledge about the individual characters' degree of criminal implication does retroactively affect your choices at the different decisive moments of the game makes the second playthrough the more interesting one: if at first you might have been well-intentioned enough to help the surveillance masterminds spying on your fellow citizens, you might be more inclined to rather try sabotaging the system on second thought, at the risk of course, to become yourself a "target" at the end.
That the game makes you second-guessing your "datachunk" choices is its biggest achievement, but that your superiors leave it entirely to you to distinguish between important and irrelevant information is Orwell's patent weakness since too ingenuous fiction-wise, though you need to contribute pertinent data in order to make the story progress, what can also be taxing at times. 
It might not exactly be a totalitarian setting but it still is shocking to realize that the monitoring of both telephone and Internet communications is something also the citizens of democratic countries are faced with, and the game does a good job in showing the use of this type of top-down espionage. Worse still, it is yourself who is doing that closed-circuit observation with Orwell as your user interface: only once a person becomes a “target” related data can be extracted from the different documents and uploaded to Orwell's servers. 
Orwell's approach might be simplified but it likely is how tracking persons in the Cyber Era does work, even when using a variety of sites, personas, and devices. This way the very conflict between public security issues and private data protection is well laid out, albeit far less preoccupying than in the famous Orwellian dystopia. 
The five different episodes can be replayed separately for the different endings, though repeatedly going through the same dialogues quickly loses its interest during replay. Given the subject's topical interest there might be stuff enough for a sequel, unless your investigations did lead to Orwell being canceled altogether...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]tl;dr:[/b] The description doesn't make clear that this is a visual novel. Don't expect much decision making, or even actual deduction--[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] holds your hand throughout the experience. If you can forgive that, and stomach the occasionally doubleplusungood prose, you'll have a decent (if predictable) exploration of surveillance. Modestly recommended; only buy during sales.

-

It's the World Of Tomorrow™, and an enigmatic nation known only as, well, The Nation is preparing the implementation of an as of yet unannounced surveillance program. With the Orwell AI on your side, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a terrorist attack, so that the government can prove the efficacy of the program and rally the support of the public. But things are not as they seem, and what was supposed to be a simple case quickly spirals out of control.

Actual gameplay, if it can be called that, mostly consists of diving into the digital lives of target persons. Now and then, the AI will highlight processable pieces of information, which are known as datachunks. If you feed a datachunk to the system, it will be sent to a government advisor on the other end of the line, who can then use the evidence to justify an arrest, call in a special ops team, et cetera. Because the advisor only gets to see those datachunks that you choose to process, he can't really read the information in its proper context, allowing you to paint a misleading picture through selectivity. By (ab)using this indirect influence, you can steer the turn of events into your preferred direction.

The idea sounds interesting enough on paper, and admittedly, it sometimes is--when the game is at its best, your choices really [i]do[/i] feel as if they matter. More often than not, though, you just go down a funnel, with your advisor telling you what to do for every step of the way. Events are supposed to happen in real-time, but are actually tied to your storyline progress; after something significant has happened, events will usually grind to a halt until you've passed some checkpoint. This implementation strips the concept of much of its strength, and it would be nice if Osmotic Studios had been a tad bit more honest about this. Indeed, I went in with a much more sandboxy expectation. Buyer, beware: [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a glorified visual novel, with no real interaction beyond some scripted points of divergence. I don't think that is necessarily a bad thing. I [i]do[/i] think it is important to know.

Another thing that cheapens the experience is the implausible interface of the AI. From time to time, you will encounter two contradictory datachunks, but instead of doing the sensible thing (uploading them both for later review), the AI will [i]force[/i] you to make a choice, even if you don't have nearly enough context to do so informedly. For some reason, these uploads can't be reversed if you find better information down the road. Even more questionably, the AI can somehow [i]know[/i] that a certain datachunk will contradict with another, even if the contradicting datachunk hasn't been found yet! I understand that these things are necessary for gameplay purposes--calling the shots in solving contradictions is one of the key ways to manipulate your advisor--but they really do shatter one's immersion.

So far, I have been pretty negative about this game, so you might be wondering why I still recommend it. The reason is quite simple: the story, is well worth experiencing. Characters feel like real, actual people who could be living next door, not like empty robots who are just there to advance the plot. And it is the very lack of meaningful choice that allowed the writers to go this far: most games are wide but shallow, [i]Orwell[/i] is narrow but deep. Granted, the attempts to make the player question their own morality mostly fall flat (contrary to what the reviewer consensus seems to be, good and evil are clear from the start), and the social commentary that permeates the writing has a distinct feeling of 'heard it all before'. There is also an overreliance on deus ex machina, particularly near the end of the story. But the characters and their various interactions are captivating enough to make you genuinely care about their fates. You might even find yourself on the edge of your seat, even though you never get to see the action directly. In my opinion, that more than makes up for the cheap plot devices, as well as the [i]very[/i] variable quality of the prose. The many references to George Orwell's [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i] add to the charm.

In short, [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a mediocre game, but with a respectable narrative. As long as you keep your expectations in check, it will certainly provide an afternoon of entertainment.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm surprised how lukewarm a lot of the reviews of this game are - I thought it was phenomenal! I guess it's because the game is mostly reading?

The government has created a piece of software designed to spy on anyone and everyone with the aim of catching criminals and terrorists. You are recruited as an investigator tasked with using it to create profiles of suspicious individuals, going through their emails, phones, desktops, etc... aiming to find anything incriminating.

Although it might seem obvious that an all-powerful piece of spying software may be somewhat unethical, Orwell does a great job at making you [i]experience[/i] it. When you're listening in on a suspect's phone call and rather than anything incriminating you just hear an argument between a couple going through a hard time in their relationship, you feel kinda gross. When you label somebody as angry and hateful based on a blog post they wrote years ago, which you later found out they regret, you get a pit in your stomach realising that the profile you made of them could have a big negative impact on this person's life in the future.

Saying that, the game doesn't feel preachy. You [i]are[/i] able to use the software to hunt down and reveal criminals who may have otherwise gone scot-free, and the game makes it clear that increased surveillance [i]is[/i] leading to dramatic reductions in crime. So does that make the gross invasion of privacy ultimately justified?? I really enjoyed how conflicted I felt up to the very end and how much it made me think.

This is a game where your choices really do matter, different people may live, die, or be arrested in your playthrough based on the choices that you make. I actually replayed the final chapter a second time because I wasn't satisfied with my ending, and managed to unlock a lot of extra information I didn't get the first time. 

I was super gripped the whole way through and am excited to play the sequel now!

It's no coincidence that this game is released few days after I finished reading 1984...

In the game, it is not (yet?) the oppressed society of Oceania portrayed in 1984 but something much closer to today's headline of mass surveillance and data collection by intelligence agencies. Big Brother is watching...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Finished in 3 hours, did not replay to look for alternate choices.

You play as a character who works for the government and has complete access to internet, phone calls, text messages, etc. Your job is to investigate people, collect evidence, and solve (and prevent) terrorist crimes. You're the man behind the camera in the all-seeing surveillance state. 

The way the surveillance system is set up is that you collect the information and pass it to an analyst. The analyst looks at the information and decides whether it is sufficient to arrest somebody, or enough to indicate another person is a person of interest that you're allowed to investigate. Over time the network of people you're investigating grows, and it's harder to keep track of their history and relationionships.

If you collect the correct information, you might be able to prevent terrorist attacks. It is possible to get enough evidence to arrest people who aren't actually dangerous or ringleaders.

Sometimes, you see conflicting information (such as when one person is lying) and you need to make a decision. You can't submit both pieces of evidence, you can't delete evidence once you've submitted it (silly, but a game mechanic to make your choices more meaningful), and sometimes it's not clear which one is correct. You sometimes can dig around and find out which piece is correct, but sometimes you need to go with your gut and what you think the people's motivations are. 

Other times, it's not clear that you're making a choice. You can always choose to submit or not submit information, and it could lead to different results. The only way to know this is to replay the game and deliberately not choose things that led to bad outcomes. At first I was just grabbing and submitting all the information I saw, but you're intended to put a bit more thought into it. Is this relevent information? Do you want the analyist making a decision based on this information? Is this quote being taken out of context? Are you encouraging your analyist to arrest a harmless person?

My only complaint about the game is [spoiler] there is only one case/group you get to investigate, and that investigation turns "meta" at the end -- having discovered the ORWELL system you're using to spy on them, they start interacting with you directly. I kind of wanted to see the system working as intended for a few cases before the "finale" case where your subjects figure out what's going on.[/spoiler] I know it's a smaller indie type of game, but a few more cases to establish what you're doing, how significant your choices are, and so on BEFORE it reached that point would have been appreciated.

I did enjoy this game. It involves a lot of reading, and a lot of thinking, in order to enjoy it properly. It's not a good game for people who want to click through the boring stuff to get to the exciting part. In a way, it's more akin to the visual novel genre than it is to more traditional games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell was an interesting experience, with a lot of potential and promise. I will say that I did enjoy the game for the most part, however, there are some glaring details which ruined it for me. 

The game relies on you (the investigator) uploading particular parsed sections of text to the server (Orwell), which means that whenever you come across a piece of information which is a "trigger" for want of a better term, it is highlighted - regardless of its relivence (and some information is totally surplus to requirement, a lot in one case). This means that most of the information which you read through, including important plot points, or interesting backstory, is largely irrelivent and the player (or at least I did) found myself just slowly scrolling to the bottom of every document to highlight all the options before I read anything at all. This is especially clear when investigating information which contradicts other information which has not been disclosed yet (marked by yellow highlighting instead of blue), as it will always be yellow, even if you have access to but haven't discovered the other piece of information yet - which unless the investigator is psychic, makes zero sense. A shame, since this dulls enthusiasm for what could otherwise be an engaging plot.

While processing this information you are presented with multiple occasions where information would be important to the case, but you cannot add it to your current file or create a new file because the game is not ready for you to do so. You will then later come back to re-read and submit this data after the game tells you the information you already noticed is important. This is irritating and makes the player feel like mommy is holding their hand through the entire experience, rather than allowing them to work on their own initiative. Although on reflection, this is most likely because the order in which the data is presented to you is not well organised from a storytelling perspective.

Attention to detail is somewhat lacking for a detective game also, as on multiple occasions you are directed to a forum which is occasionally updated with new articles to peruse. Unfortunately, when these articles are "published" the game does not update the "last logged in" sections of the user's profiles, which creates confusion over the timeline [spoiler]especially since this becomes important later in the story[/spoiler].

However, the largest problem is that there are several key events which the game does not provide you enough information to correctly answer (and there is a correct answer), which leads to the player essentially taking a wild guess as to which of the options is the correct one. If you are fortunate, you will get the result which you were looking for - if not... well you'll have to go through the entire game again from the beginning, as the game auto-saves after every piece of information you upload.

Overall, Orwell is a thought-provoking and mostly enjoyable game, but it does have it's flaws. If you can overlook them however, you will appreciate the intention of the developer. At this point I have to decide if I recommend Orwell or not, and it is difficult... 

8/10. Would not play again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is, as you might guess from the title, a near-future dystopian terrorism thriller told through the lens of the titular national surveillance system of a fictional country called simply The Nation. You learn about the characters through their chat logs, social media and blog posts etcetera and slowly build up a picture of what is going on. But will it be the right picture, or will it lead to more bombings? Will the guilty parties get arrested or will law enforcement focus on the wrong targets? All this and more is up to you, as a faceless "investigator" assigned to the Orwell mass surveillance project.

It looks like it was originally released episodically but it works just as well playing it all the way through. But remember: the system only makes connections based on the data YOU upload to it. If you pick the wrong information, things can go sideways very badly.

I picked this game up in the Christmas 2016 sale and have enjoyed my first playthrough greatly, so I highly recommend it for anyone looking for a story and character driven thriller of this kind. Do be prepared for a lot of clicking, scrolling and dragging and dropping though.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Excellent game, thoroughly enjoyed it.  Basically everything would be a spoiler so I'm not going to mention anything game specific, but it plays out like a text-based Telltale game.  Also meta, but not in an obnoxious way - I appreciate that.

As for critiques, it was very irritating to discover information prior to being allowed to select, even when you *know* it is pertinent to the investigation. It felt like too much handholding (with pre-highlighted phrases), and too many bottlenecks stopping me from filling out my investigation at my own pace.  AND LET PLAYERS ZOOM OUT ON THE CONNECTIONS/CONTACTS MAP! It was infuriating scrolling around.  Also, from an intelligence standpoint, the paths to other persons in the contact networks should be labelled with their relationship (Brother, Sister, Girlfriend, etc.) and updated as you discover more information just like everything else. 

Cosmetic Bug: The player can choose which primary profile picture they associate with each person, which changes that picture in all subsequent documents or interactions (calls, texts), but during one scripted cutscene it defaulted to what would probably have been the newest picture I had discovered (Nina in this case) when I had purposely switched to a prior picture. No one would normally notice, but it is still a jarring bug because they were very different pictures and it didn't make logical sense with the way I was building the narrrative for Orwell.
